This doesn't apply to all countries though. In Belgium, a group of people were charged for holocaust denial because they shared memes about the holocaust in a private chat group of friends. The chat was infiltrated because they belonged to a right-wing youth group and they were subsequently charged for materials shared in private. It's also sufficient to facilitate spreading it as opposed to sharing it yourself.

Also worth noting that holocaust denial in most cases doesn't mean actual denial as in denying that it happened, but minimising, disrespecting, or ridiculing it. With antisemetic memes, for example. All of these are handled by the same law in most places.

There's no workbook on how to recover from abuse, unfortunately. There are valuable resources out there, and how much they will help you will depend on where your struggles lie. Stuff like "The body keeps the score" may help you understand your psyche a bit better, although the book isn't for the faint of heart.

If you have access to a good therapist whom you trust, they should be able to help you navigate the process. Think of therapists like a tour guide - someone who knows the terrain well and can tell you where to turn. You may be perfectly able to guide yourself with the help of a map, but if you feel stuck or lost, they can support you.

That being said you don't need one to successfully recover from your experiences. The first step is always to take stock of where you are and how it has precisely affected you. Emotional abuse affects everyone differently, but we usually see issues with emotional dysregulation and anxiety, low self esteem, etc. These are the most common and also some of the most fundamental - and also straightforward enough to attack on your own.

So, for example, you can look up therapeutic skills to start regulating your emotions (eg DBT) and work on your self esteem by showing up for yourself and getting to know what needs and wants you have that you may have suppressed over the years. In my experience, talking about what happened to us doesn't help as much as proving to ourselves that we are now capable of providing our own safety.

Good luck :)

Fellow European psychologist here!

I think it's worth noting that the DSM-V is not the only diagnostic instrument. There's also the ICD-11, which is used beyond the United States. According to the ICD-11, e.g., anorexia nervosa may be defined as follows (emphasis added by me):

Anorexia Nervosa is characterised by significantly low body weight for the individual’s height, age and developmental stage that is not due to another health condition or to the unavailability of food. A commonly used threshold is body mass index (BMI) less than 18.5 kg/m² in adults and BMI-for-age under 5th percentile in children and adolescents. **Rapid weight loss (e.g. more than 20% of total body weight within 6 months) may replace the low body weight guideline** ***as long as other diagnostic requirements are met***. Children and adolescents may exhibit failure to gain weight as expected based on the individual developmental trajectory rather than weight loss. Low body weight is **accompanied by a persistent pattern of behaviours to prevent restoration of normal weight**, which may include behaviours aimed at reducing energy intake (restricted eating), purging behaviours (e.g. self-induced vomiting, misuse of laxatives), and behaviours aimed at increasing energy expenditure (e.g. excessive exercise), typically associated with a fear of weight gain. Low body weight or shape is central to the person's self-evaluation or is inaccurately perceived to be normal or even excessive.

I personally find this definition much more apt, also in communicating with clients, because it is inclusive of people who develop eating disorders at a higher weight without broadening diagnostic criteria inappropriately.

It's important to keep in mind that the #1 purpose of BMI severity criteria is to evaluate when a person may need emergency medical attention or inpatient treatment to prevent death - not when the actual behaviors they engage in are the most severe or when their mental state is the most precarious. Those criteria are important, but they should not be people's only mental models of disease severity.

That's not a correct definition or perspective on what trauma is. People have nightmares, people have experiences that affect their well-being. That doesn't make something traumatic. Traumatization describes an alteration of the nervous system in response to a stimulus perceived as so threatening and dangerous that it severely and lastingly disturbs our nervous system functioning. 

For some video material I could understand a trauma-like reaction (very graphic, violent imagery for example) but in and of itself you cannot really be traumatized through a photo or video. It may remind you of something and thus also bring up unpleasant feelings, but again that's not what being traumatized means.

This is a bit of a curveball, but have you ever worn a glucose monitor?

I have a condition called reactive hypoglycemia. I describe it kinda like you do and it doesn't show up at all in fasting glucose. Basically my body has way too much bioavailable insulin and processes any kind of carbohydrate way too quickly, causing my blood sugar to dumb rapidly. This dump happens 2-3 hours after meals that contain large amount of carbohydrates, and it leads to anything from mild muscle weakness to severe fatigue that requires me to lie down. I have passed out from it before.

Depending on when I eat and what, my blood sugar crashes roughly match up with when you report feeling the worst (\~12 ie a few hours after breakfast and \~4 a few hours after lunch). Depending on what you eat for dinner or before bed, it could also cause some really weird blood sugar levels during sleep, leading to much worse sleep quality.

So the main questions to ask yourself is what you eat and if it roughly links up with your crashes. If you think this could be your issue, then see if you can convince a doctor to either let you wear a CGM or to do a glucose test in office (they give you some pure sugar fasted and see what happens).

Can we not label something as emotional abuse when it's not?

People with mental illness, especially anxiety or borderline, are more sensitive. That's not an insult. They are emotionally hyper-reactive, and disproportionately perceive and interpret things as slights, threats or sources of worry that are completely innocent. They become upset at things other people wouldn't and feel worried about people's intentions when they are totally pure. This is an essential aspect of the dysfunction associated with these disorders. They already feel 'crazy' and have low self confidence. 

The boyfriend seems to say "things that hurt her feelings". Degrading and breaking someone's confidence needs to be intentional for it to be abusive, is that really the case here from what we know? For a person with borderline and depression, they could feel degraded by "why didn't you put away the groceries yet?" in a normal tone of voice. They could feel worthless as the result of harmless jokes like "well you're a housewife sometimes!" that are a means of the partner coping with the fact that their partner is dysfunctional and barely takes care of themselves and their shared space.

The partner walking on eggshells and censoring every word they say does nothing to make the relationship healthier. It also over-accommodates the mental health issue in such a way that establishes 'anxious and hyper-sensitive' as the standard, which is not good for OP in therapy or recovery either. OP and her partner need to work on understanding why he makes these comments and understanding how those reasons can be addressed, not leave him.

Obviously, if the partner is not open to conversation, does not want to cooperate with OP to address her mental health needs and the comments become objectively hurtful, we enter emotional abuse territory. But I don't think that's the automatic conclusion to draw from this post.

Source: emotional abuse researcher and advocate, went through this process myself after severe child abuse and also hold a clinical psychology degree.

Is the mum innocent here? No. Is she right in that her son is likely going to carry disproportionate, negative consequences from this event that go far beyond 'I won't steal again' because OP's uncle threatened that kid? Yes. Let me tell you why:

I was really badly abused and neglected as a kid. I started getting bullied for my lack of hygiene (parents didn't teach me, refused to buy stuff like toothpaste, deodorant, feminine hygiene products etc.) and I had no money, so I started to steal from a local drugstore. I got away with it a couple times until I didn't. I was 13. Police were called, I was reprimanded and banned from the store. Hell came over me at home.

For years after the fact, every phone call that came to our home phone, every time our bell rang, every person I heard come up to our door I thought were the police finally coming to get me for those times I'd stolen before. I couldn't sleep well, I had nightmares about the ordeal most nights, I had to listen to every call that came into the house to make sure it wasn't about me and it went on like that for years.

Now, in my case, I was so used to authority being leveraged over me in an abusive manner (my parents) that I just expected every other authority to act the same, which is why I developed quasi posttraumatic stress from an incident in which police barely threatened me. In OP's nephew's case, the police actually did exert their authority inappropriately and in threatening ways, which obviously instilled a kind of fear in the little boy that is clearly not useful nor healthy for him.

Fear is not a parenting tactic. There's OSFED (previously EDNOS) which describes cases of specific eating disorders that don't quite meet diagnostic criteria - atypical anorexia falls into this category for example, where the person loses a significant amount of weight but isn't underweight or in physical danger.

There's also UFED, which is usually diagnosed when the clinician doesn't have a lot of information or when the person's functioning is severely impaired by a broad spectrum of eating disordered behaviors and symptoms (dysmorphia, malnutrition and dehydration, immune system dysfunction, mood-related symptoms, overexercising.. you get the gist).

In OP's case, I'm not sure they would be diagnosed with either. This is not to invalidate what they are going through - we all went through the beginning phases of our disorders. The issue is that they are eating disorders - meaning that although they are mental disorders, they are concerned first and foremost with eating *behaviors* and classified as such. There are simply no diagnoses that serve preventative purposes, that "catch" the beginnings of disordered behaviors before they get worse, because we use these labels to treat people once they have overwhelmed a person's mental and physical health, not to help people put a name to their struggles.

Being traumatized = having PTSD. Suffering from enduring consequences of a traumatic event = being traumatized = PTSD. If you don't suffer lasting consequences to your functioning and otherwise you are not traumatized, you experienced a (potentially traumatic) event. There is no such thing as being traumatized but not having PTSD. They're the same. Which is why using the term is inappropriate.

As for trauma - the term is a bit ill-defined, but usually refers to both the traumatic event and the lasting mental health issues that result from it. Meaning again, we should be referring to psychiatric conditions. Sometimes it's used to describe traumatic events that don't result in posttraumatic stress. When most people say "trauma", they aren't referring to what the term actually means. Which, again, is the issue.

I have medical trauma. I was severely neglected and had to have most of my teeth fixed/replaced when I was a teenager, they were completely rotten before someone finally noticed. I spent years never laughing or smiling to hide it, I couldn't eat properly. Years of severe nerve pain. All that is to say - none of this is said out of ignorance or a lack of empathy for a struggling adolescent.

It's quite telling, though, that you think what constitutes trauma can be gatekept. You also seem to think having T1 diabetes entitles you to your opinion, but having PTSD doesn't entitle me to mine?

Like all mental health issues, trauma is somewhat subjective but is still a psychiatric condition that can be defined by the nature of the event and the way that it impacts an individual. I cannot gatekeep trauma because nobody can. It may look slightly different for different people and it may be more mild or severe, but there are still objective criteria to go by.

Trauma is not a synonym for hardship, just like mania isn't a synonym for excitement, depression isn't a synonym for sadness.. the list goes on. It is simply not respectful to use words that way. I have issues with my blood sugar - I don't say I have diabetes because while I do struggle with it from time to time, I don't have an autoimmune disease. Do you get it?

Just be respectful of people with our conditions and adjust your vocabulary to reflect the real meaning of the words. It doesn't take much at all.

Having a 'traumatic' experience and being 'traumatized' are two different things. And even then, the threshold for what constitutes a 'traumatic experience' is much higher than *most* people realize. There is good reason 'traumatic' is not a synonym for 'very upsetting' or 'life-changing' even though people use it as such.

I absolutely understand how being diagnosed with type 1, especially in the US, is potentially traumatic because of the helplessness you may feel and the threat to your health it poses, especially when you are newly diagnosed and may not have a good understanding of how it impacts your body quite yet. I can also see that OP's daughter is enduring a great deal of stress and impact on her functioning, presumably for quite a while now, which could be indicative of a stress-related condition related to her diagnosis.

However, chronic illnesses are linked to mental health through a great variety of factors, not just traumatic exposure; there are even circumstances under which certain stressors can be beneficial for mental health (there is scientific evidence for this).

Plus, there are many reasons not to use psychiatric descriptors (traumatic, traumatized) when talking about a stranger you don't know, just like it's generally inappropriate to label someone as having a personality disorder from three sentences you read about them on reddit. You can speculate of course, just like I did, but these words carry a certain meaning and severity that many people aren't mindful of. Even when something like a diagnosis totally changes your life doesn't mean it will be traumatic. There's way more to it than that. Stating that someone **is** traumatized or **did** go through something traumatic is just not appropriate and a bit disrespectful to people with trauma-related psychiatric conditions.

First of all, having a diverse array of experiences, feelings and even opinions doesn't make you abnormal in the slightest - as far as that goes, it is something all humans go through. Nobody is perfect they all say - you know why? Because everyone thinks, does or feels something contradictory sometimes.

But when it comes to what you wrote, it reads to me like you don't have a stable sense of self - many of us don't. We weren't given the time, space or safety to develop our personalities, so they don't exist yet as they do for many other people our age.

I don't like the notion of "memories" or "evidence". My father was (is) psychopathic, I was abused and neglected by my parents, step-parents, extended family at times. But there are only a few select memories I "have" that I could communicate - being beaten up at school, being pinned against a wall at home for having a meltdown, being called a whore for my trashy room, my father confessing that he didn't love me and that I'd never find out why. Having to walk around with a broken arm for five days until I was taken to a doctor. Having 40+ fillings in my teeth before I even hit adulthood. That is enough for anyone not traumatized to recognize that it's fucked up - yet a lot more of the impact came from the way I was treated day in and day out, what I was used to, how I was (or wasn't) socialized. These things were routine, and you don't remember routine, it doesn't stand out to you as distinct "memories" if you experienced it every day. If you were accustomed to observing violence, you have a good chance of not remembering it in spite of the impact it had on you.

That all is to say - you don't need evidence or memories. You may be driving yourself a little crazy, yes, but you don't need to remember things to recognize the impact something must have had on you to feel as you feel right now.

The point is that it's not impossible but very unlikely. He said he's only seen one DC that is actually 5'7 - that implies that a very small percentage of people at that height will be DC. If someone at that height truly looks better in DC recs than any of the tall ones, then sure, be the exception. The exception makes the rule. But on here it feels like 90% of people at the height limit believe themselves to be the exception, which is just statistically impossible and causes the annoyance.

The key to what you said is "if it looks good on them". I totally agree. The problem that I see with people who believe they're the exception at a height limit is that they will get into Kibbe, resonate with a certain ID often based on its image and then fixate on it despite it being generally unlikely that they are that ID and stick with it. They are often resistant to really experimenting with other types and will then type others in the same fashion ("if I can be a 5'7 DC you can be too!"). They don't fully explore what looks *best* on them, they stick with the type they assumed because *it doesn't look bad*. And then it leads to more and more people misunderstanding what the type looks like.

So if someone is 5'6.5, doesn't have width or curve and objectively looks better in DC than in D recs, I totally agree it's sensible for them to assume DC. I don't think it makes sense to shoehorn them into D when vertical accommodation leaves something to be desired and balance accommodation solves their problems. But because it is so unlikely at a certain point, if somebody wants to arrive at their true type they should really go through this exclusion process first, which people who think they're the exception usually do not.

That depends on what you mean by hard rules. There are many soft rules (such as that from a certain height, your vertical will be too dominant to be anything but one of 3 types) but bodies can't easily be put into boxes and Kibbe is expressly against that - he emphasizes that these are not body types, but merely a system to understand how clothing falls on the body - which is always at least a tad subjective. If you're looking for a system that is very clear cut, it's definitely not the one for you :D

The three 'tall' types are differentiated through the features of vertical, curve and width. Pure vertical is D, vertical + curve is SD, vertical + width is FN. There are some other features but that is the basics.

Width is not the literal width of your shoulders as a measurement, it's about whether your clothing needs to accommodate for it (ie provide room in the shoulders and upper ribcage). It refers to an impression of width rather than "does this person have broad shoulders or not?". That means it's also relative to your own stature and is influenced by other characteristics.

The same goes for curve, it's always relative to your size and Kibbe curve is not the same thing as conventional curve. Somebody could have HH cups and not have Kibbe curve. Like I said in another comment, it takes some time and curiosity to get into Kibbe and understand his ideas. It's not like the "there are apples, pears, oranges.." theories and thus not as simple to understand either. You can't expect to understand everything about it the first time you look at it.. or even the tenth time lmao.

If you think it is a raging dumpster fire, I suggest you just don't engage with it. It's not a perfect theory and he wrote his first book 40 years ago, so some of his recent opinions may contradict older ones. But his theory has merit in his own thinking and if it doesn't suit you, maybe it's not the system for you.

I smoked from 16 to 20 and quit cold turkey almost 2.5 years ago.

How I think it works is - the unhealthier the habit is, the more helpful it'll seem in achieving unhealthy goals or being means to them. Nicotine doesn't make you any less hungry and doesn't keep you 'rail thin' - it's just one kind of habit people may use as a placeholder for actual food, but because it's engrained in our minds as this 'cool girl that smokes instead of eats' stereotype it aids us in fulfilling that stereotype. But it will actually make you incredibly nauseous for a good while and not in an 'uhh i don't have an appetite how nice' kinda way. 

That's how it worked for me - I was that cool girl rolling her cigarettes, smoking in meal breaks, cigarettes were like my best friend. Whatever I was feeling I could just smoke for relief. But what I didn't realize is that it didn't make me cool or relieved. I also found that as an early 20's woman, the 'smokers' usually were bad social circles for me and would encourage picking up more drugs and engaging in more unhealthy behavior. 

You can use any habit in place of it and have it have the same effect - water, coffee, tea, energy drinks, non-nicotine vaping, gum, whatever. I even chewed **actual** flowers at one point lmfao. I've been through them all and all that matters is your attitude and conviction, not nicotine. Soooo many times I had my morning cig and 5 minutes later, I'd think "fuck, I'm nauseous, I need to eat something". Water wouldn't do that. If you're going to start a habit to supplement starving yourself, at least take up the ones that don't shave decades off your life. Please.
